questions.q: In the BookStore, what does POST /sessions do?
questions.explain: Register is POST /users. Log in is POST /sessions, which answers with a token. After that, every protected request proves who it is by sending the token in the Authorization header.
options: It stores a new user's e-mail and password hash
It checks the e-mail and password and returns a signed token
It returns the list of logged-in users
It checks the token on every protected request

questions.q: Where does the token-signing secret come from?
questions.explain: Anyone who has the secret can make tokens for any user, so it never goes into the code or into git. loadConfig reads it from the environment and fails fast if it is missing or too short.
options: A constant in src/auth/token.ts, so every server uses the same one
A secret.txt file committed next to the code
The TOKEN_SECRET environment variable, and the server refuses to start without a good one
It is generated from the user's password

questions.q: Why does loadConfig refuse TOKEN_SECRET=secret?
questions.explain: A secret is only safe if nobody can guess it. randomBytes(32).toString("hex") gives 64 random characters. A missing secret and a short one are both refused.
options: Because secrets must be written in hex
Because a short, guessable secret lets an attacker guess it and forge tokens; it must be a random value of at least 32 characters
Because a secret must contain digits and symbols
It does not; any non-empty value is accepted

questions.q: Which is the right way to handle token secrets?
questions.explain: A secret that has been seen elsewhere is not a secret. If it leaks, replacing it makes every token signed with the old one stop working, which is exactly what you want.
options: Copy the secret from the tutorial so everyone's examples match
Use one secret for development, testing and production, so tokens work everywhere
Make a fresh random secret for each environment, and replace it if it ever leaks
Share it in the team chat so nobody gets locked out

questions.q: Why does the users table store a password hash and not the password?
questions.explain: A hash is the output of a one-way function. You can check a password against it, but not recover the password from it. Nobody, not even you, should be able to read users' passwords.
options: Because hashes are shorter
If the database leaks, the attacker must not learn the passwords; a hash cannot be turned back into the password
Because PostgreSQL cannot store passwords
So the server can e-mail users their password

questions.q: Why is a fast hash like SHA-256 the wrong tool for passwords?
questions.explain: Speed helps the attacker, who tries guess after guess against the stolen hashes. scrypt makes each guess expensive, while one check at log-in is still quick enough for a real user.
options: Because it produces hashes that are too long
Because an attacker with a leaked hash can try billions of guesses per second; password hashes like scrypt are slow on purpose
Because SHA-256 is not built into Node.js
Because SHA-256 can be reversed

questions.q: What does the random salt in hashPassword achieve?
questions.explain: Each password gets its own salt, and the salt is stored next to the key: scrypt$salt$key. The same password hashed twice gives different strings, yet both verify correctly.
options: It makes the password longer, so it is harder to guess
Two users with the same password get different hashes, so one cracked hash does not reveal the others
It encrypts the password so the server can read it back
It replaces the need for a slow hash

questions.q: Why does verifyPassword compare with timingSafeEqual instead of ===?
questions.explain: timingSafeEqual always takes the same time, wherever the values differ. It throws when the lengths differ, which is why the code checks actual.length === expected.length first.
options: Because === cannot compare buffers of the same length
A normal comparison stops at the first different byte, and an attacker can measure that time to guess a value piece by piece
Because timingSafeEqual is faster
Because === would ignore upper and lower case

questions.q: What does the HMAC signature on a BookStore token protect against?
questions.explain: The signature is a hash of the content mixed with the secret. Change one character and it no longer matches; without the secret, nobody can make a new one. It does not hide the content.
options: Anyone reading the token's content
Anyone changing the content or making a new valid token without the secret
The token being sent over plain HTTP
The user forgetting to log out

questions.q: A token's payload part decodes to {"sub":7,"exp":1790168400}. What follows from this?
questions.explain: base64url is just a way to write bytes as text; it is not encryption. The signature stops changes, not reading. Keep only what is needed, like the user id and the expiry.
options: The token is broken: payloads should be encrypted
Anyone can read a token, so never put a password or other private data in it
Only the server can decode it, because of the signature
The user id should be removed, since it is visible

questions.q: In the token payload, what are sub and exp?
questions.explain: The payload says who and until when. A BookStore token lives one hour; readToken refuses it once exp * 1000 <= now.
options: sub is the session id; exp is the time the token was created
sub is the subject (the user id); exp is when it expires, in seconds since 1970
sub is the signature; exp is the secret's expiry
sub is the e-mail; exp is the time the user logged in

questions.q: Why do createToken and readToken take now = Date.now() as a parameter?
questions.explain: Time is an outside dependency, like the fake clock in Classes in TypeScript. The default uses the real time, while tests pass fixed times and get the same result on every run.
options: Because Date.now() is not allowed inside a module
So a test can pass any time it likes: "two hours later" does not mean waiting two hours
So the client can choose when its token expires
To make tokens from different servers match

questions.q: Why does log-in answer Wrong e-mail or password both when the e-mail is unknown and when the password is wrong?
questions.explain: Different messages would let anyone test a list of e-mail addresses and learn who uses the shop. One message for both cases gives them nothing.
options: Because the server cannot tell the two cases apart
So the answer does not tell a stranger which e-mails have accounts
Because 401 only allows one message
To save one database query

questions.q: A logged-in client sends {"bookId": 1, "quantity": 1, "userId": 2} to POST /orders. Where must the order's user id come from?
questions.explain: If the client could name the user, any logged-in user could order in someone else's name or read their orders by changing a number. Only the signed token proves who is calling.
options: From body.userId, because the client knows who it is
From body.userId, but only if it matches an existing user
Only from the verified token, through requireUserId; parseNewOrder has no userId field at all
From a userId query string

questions.q: A client calls GET /orders with no Authorization header. What does requireUserId do?
questions.explain: No token, a bad signature and an expired token all mean "we do not know who you are": 401. The route never runs, so nobody's orders are shown.
options: Returns user id 0, a guest
Returns every order, since no user is given
Throws an HttpError 401 Unauthorized, telling the client to log in and send a Bearer token
Throws a 404, because there are no orders for nobody

questions.q: Which rule does parseCredentials follow?
questions.explain: Ada@Example.com and ada@example.com are one account. A password is used exactly as typed, but its length is checked (10 to 200 characters).
options: It trims and lower-cases both the e-mail and the password
It lower-cases the e-mail, but does not trim the password, because spaces are allowed in a password
It lower-cases the password so users can type it in any case
It accepts any password length, because the hash has a fixed length

questions.q: UserRepository.create runs INSERT … RETURNING id, email and returns a User with no hash. Why?
questions.explain: Build what you send from chosen fields. The hash is only read in one place, where it is needed, and never sent to a client.
options: Because the hash is not stored
The result goes straight into the 201 response, and a hash must never leave the server; only findByEmail returns it, for the log-in check
Because RETURNING cannot return text columns
To make the query faster

questions.q: What is still missing to protect POST /sessions from a script trying a million passwords?
questions.explain: A public log-in route needs a rate limit. The lesson lists it among the missing security layers. The Rate limiting lesson builds one, and ZudoJS provides one in @zudojs/security.
options: A longer token lifetime
Returning a different message for unknown e-mails
A rate limit: only a few log-in attempts per minute per client
Hashing the password twice

questions.q: The token tests start with const secret = randomBytes(32).toString("hex"). Why not paste the real TOKEN_SECRET into the test file?
questions.explain: No real secret ever appears in a test file. The tests only need a secret, and a fresh random one checks the same rules.
options: Because tests run faster with a random secret
A test file is committed to git, so a real secret there would leak; each run makes its own throwaway secret
Because readToken only accepts hex secrets
Because the real secret changes every hour

questions.q: The honest review says the router has no middleware. What is the risk that follows?
questions.explain: Security that depends on remembering a line in each handler fails the first time someone forgets. A framework can attach the check to a whole group of routes in one place.
options: Routes cannot be async
"Require a user" is a line you must remember in every protected handler; forget it once and that route is open to everyone
The router cannot tell 404 from 405
Tokens cannot be read without middleware

questions.q: Why does the review say the BookStore has no real log-out?
questions.explain: The server checks only the signature and the expiry. A stolen token keeps working for up to an hour. Revoking tokens needs extra state on the server, one of the security layers still missing.
options: Because there is no DELETE /sessions route yet, and adding one fixes it
A signed token stays valid until it expires; the server keeps no list, so it cannot revoke a token early
Because the client deletes its token automatically
Because tokens never expire

questions.q: readToken starts with const [data, signature, extra] = token.split("."). What does this print?
questions.explain: A BookStore token is exactly data.signature. With no dot, signature is undefined; with a third part, extra exists. Anything that is not exactly two parts is refused before any other work.
options: two parts rejected rejected rejected
two parts rejected two parts rejected
two parts two parts rejected rejected
two parts rejected rejected two parts

questions.q: What does this print?

options: abc.def undefined undefined undefined
abc.def abc.def undefined undefined
Bearer abc.def undefined undefined undefined
abc.def undefined undefined YWRh

questions.q: readToken refuses a token when payload.exp * 1000 <= now. What does this print?
questions.explain: exp is in seconds and now in milliseconds, hence the * 1000. At exactly 5 minutes the token is already expired, because the check uses <=. A 5-minute token is fine after 4 minutes and refused after 6.
options: true false false
true true false
false false false
true true true

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each user sees only their own orders, filtered by the id from the verified token. The bodyUserId is simply never used. A user with no orders gets an empty list, not everybody's orders.

questions.q:
Extend loadConfig(env) so it also reads TOKEN_SECRET. If the secret is missing or shorter than 32 characters, throw an Error with the message TOKEN_SECRET must be set to a random value of at least 32 characters. The program should print:

TOKEN_SECRET must be set to a random value of at least 32 characters
TOKEN_SECRET must be set to a random value of at least 32 characters
3000 40
questions.explain: The server must refuse to start without a good secret, before it opens a port. The error names the setting but never prints the secret's value.
questions.expected:
TOKEN_SECRET must be set to a random value of at least 32 characters
TOKEN_SECRET must be set to a random value of at least 32 characters
3000 40

questions.q: Write bearerToken(header). header is unknown (it comes from the request). Return the token when the header is a string starting with Bearer (with the space) and something follows it; otherwise return undefined. The program should print [ 'abc.def', undefined, undefined, undefined ].
questions.explain: Headers are outside input, so check the type first. Only the Bearer scheme is accepted; anything else gives no token, and the guard answers 401.

questions.q: Write the type guard isPayload(value): true only for an object with whole-number sub and exp fields. The program should print [ true, false, false, false ].
questions.explain: Even a correctly signed token's content is checked before use. Number.isInteger is false for strings like "7", and in makes sure both fields exist.

questions.q: Write isExpired(payload, now). payload.exp is in seconds; now is in milliseconds. A token is expired when exp (in milliseconds) is less than or equal to now. The program should print false true true.
questions.explain: Mixing seconds and milliseconds is a classic bug: without * 1000, every token would look expired since 1970. Passing now in makes the check easy to test at exact times.

questions.q:
Write parseCredentials(input). Lower-case and trim the e-mail; push email is not an e-mail address when it does not match /^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+$/. Keep the password exactly as sent (a string, not trimmed); push password must be 10 to 200 characters when its length is outside that range. Return { email, password, issues }. The program should print:

{"email":"ada@example.com","password":" a long passphrase ","issues":[]}
["email is not an e-mail address","password must be 10 to 200 characters"]
questions.explain: One account per e-mail means comparing e-mails in lower case. The password is never changed, only checked; a number is not a password, so it counts as empty and fails the length rule.
questions.expected:
{"email":"ada@example.com","password":" a long passphrase ","issues":[]}
["email is not an e-mail address","password must be 10 to 200 characters"]

questions.q:
Write requireUserId(headers, readToken). Take the token from headers["authorization"] (format Bearer <token>) and pass it to readToken. If there is no token or readToken returns undefined, throw new HttpError(401, "unauthorized"). Otherwise return the payload's sub. The program should print:

7
401 unauthorized
401 unauthorized
questions.explain: The user id comes only from a token that readToken accepted. A forged token and a missing header both end as 401, before the route does anything. Passing readToken in lets a test use a fake.

questions.q:
Write logIn(email, password). Look the user up with findByEmail. If there is no user, or verify(password, user.passwordHash) is false, throw new HttpError(401, "Wrong e-mail or password"): the same error for both cases. Otherwise return token-for-<id>. The program should print:

token-for-1
401 Wrong e-mail or password
401 Wrong e-mail or password
questions.explain: An unknown e-mail and a wrong password get the same answer, so a stranger cannot learn which e-mails have accounts. (The fake verify here stands in for scrypt; never store passwords like this for real.)
questions.expected:
token-for-1
401 Wrong e-mail or password
401 Wrong e-mail or password

questions.q: Write placeOrder(userId, body). userId comes from the verified token. Copy only bookId and quantity from the body, and set the order's userId from the parameter, never from the body. The program should print {"userId":1,"bookId":3,"quantity":1}.
questions.explain: The client tried to order as user 2. Because the order is built from the token's user id and two named fields, that attempt has no effect. Spreading the body would copy whatever else the client sent; listing the fields is the safe habit.

questions.q:
Write parseStored(stored) for values like scrypt$<salt>$<key>. Return { salt, key } only when there are exactly three parts, the first is scrypt, and salt and key are not empty. Otherwise return undefined, never throw. The program should print:

{"salt":"cr-RTX","key":"KW9aww"}
undefined
undefined
undefined
questions.explain: A damaged or old-format value in the database must mean "wrong password", not a crash. Checking the shape first lets verifyPassword return false safely.

questions.q: Write toPublicUser(row), which returns only id and email from a user row, never the password hash. The program should print {"id":1,"email":"ada@example.com"}.
questions.explain: Returning row itself would type-check (a UserRow has every User field) and leak the hash. Building a new object from chosen fields is the only safe way.

questions.q:
Write listFor(orders, userId). Return only the orders whose userId matches, without the userId field: { id, bookId, quantity }. The program should print:

[{"id":1,"bookId":1,"quantity":2},{"id":3,"bookId":2,"quantity":1}]
[]
questions.explain: This is WHERE user_id = $1 in memory. The userId passed in comes from the token, so each user sees only their own orders, and someone with no orders gets an empty list.
